text:
So measure it yourself. Collect real examples with known answers, run each candidate, score automatically, and compare. [curious] How many examples? Fewer than you'd think. Take one model that's right eighty percent of the time and one that's right sixty-five. Score each on twenty examples, again and again. The better one comes out ahead about four times in five. With fifty examples, ninety-four times in a hundred. And if two still look close after thirty examples, they probably are. Pick on cost.

The harness is just a loop. Here are ten tickets, each with its right queue, and two stand-in models. The cheap one routes three of them right. Thirty percent. The other gets all ten. But read the misses. The cheap one sent all seven to other. Whether that hurts depends on who reads that queue.

Free text is harder to score. First choice: make the output checkable, with fields to compare. Next: score properties. Does it name the three facts, and stay under the limit? Last: have a strong model grade it on a rubric, knowing judges favor longer answers.

Then put cost beside accuracy. Say four tiers score ninety-one to ninety-five percent on a million requests a month. Opus buys one point over Sonnet, for twice the money. Fable buys nothing over Opus, at two and a half times the price. So it comes down to what an error costs you. A minute of triage? The cheap model wins. A lost customer? It doesn't.

Build that harness once, and it outlives every model in it. When the next one launches, skip its table. Run your examples, and in an hour you'll know if it's good enough.
